title: Come apart and rest (Mark 6:30–44)
hook: come apart into a desert place, and rest a little, then the crowds, then the loaves

segments.voice: Yesterday, two by two: the twelve sent out with nothing. Your line was take nothing for the way. What did you leave behind? Today they come back, tired. Day two hundred eight.

You know the feeling after a big stretch of work. Exams done, the shift over, the move finished, the guests gone. You come home buzzing and exhausted, with a hundred stories to tell and no energy to tell them. The twelve come back from their first mission just like that. They crowd around Jesus to report everything they did and taught. And it's so busy, Mark says, with people coming and going, that they don't even have time to eat. And Jesus says one of the kindest sentences in the gospel. Today: come apart and rest.
screen: `BACK FROM A BIG STRETCH.` → `NO TIME EVEN TO EAT.` → `ONE OF THE KINDEST SENTENCES.`

segments.voice: First, the invitation. In the Douay-Rheims: "Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little. For there were many coming and going: and they had not so much as time to eat." Apart means away, by yourselves. Jesus sees tired people and prescribes rest before anything else. It's an invitation that comes from him, not a reward they've earned. Second, the crowd. They get in a boat to find a quiet place, but people see them go and run around the shore on foot, and get there first. The rest is interrupted. And Jesus, seeing the crowd, has compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. So he teaches them. Third, the loaves. It gets late. The disciples say, send them away to buy food. Jesus says: you give them something to eat. They have five loaves and two fish. He has the people sit down in groups on the green grass. Then he takes the loaves, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives them to the disciples to hand out. Everyone eats and is filled, and they gather up twelve baskets of leftovers. Five thousand men were fed. Fourth, those four verbs. Took, blessed, broke, gave. Catholics hear them again at every Mass, in the words over the bread at the Last Supper. So this meal in the desert points forward to the Eucharist. And it starts from an unfinished rest. The rest didn't fail. It was the beginning. Jesus never takes back the invitation: come apart, and rest a little.
screen: `COME APART: AWAY, BY YOURSELVES.` · `SHEEP WITHOUT A SHEPHERD.` · `FIVE LOAVES, TWO FISH.` · `TOOK, BLESSED, BROKE, GAVE.` · then, large: `COME APART INTO A DESERT PLACE, AND REST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a real break, right now. Settle, and breathe. This is your desert place. No one is coming or going for two minutes. Let your eyes close or soften. Notice how tired you actually are, without judging it. If you pray, you can hear the invitation as if it were spoken to you: come apart, and rest a little. If you don't, just rest a little, the way you'd tell a tired friend to. The bell holds the time.
Come apart and rest. Jesus's invitation to his tired friends, before the crowds and before the loaves. Today's word.
Your line: rest a little. Today, take one real break, away from the coming and going, and eat something sitting down. Day two hundred eight.

screen: `DAY 208 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IT IS I, FEAR NOT.`

howItsDone: Catholics hear the feeding of the five thousand as a sign pointing to the Eucharist, and many make retreats, days apart for prayer and rest, taking this passage as their invitation.

fork.reveal: "Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little." rest comes before anything else.

original.note: Greek: apart, privately, by yourselves, in Jesus's invitation to rest.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle about bread.
what it means: it starts with an invitation to tired friends to rest, and becomes a meal that points to the Eucharist.
what a scholar hears: kat' idian, apart; almost the only place Mark calls the twelve apostles; took, blessed, broke, gave, as at the Last Supper.

sources.quoted: Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little. For there were many coming and going: and they had not so much as time to eat.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 6:31 given from memory; confirm.
Mark 6:30 is often noted as the only (or nearly the only) place Mark uses 'apostles' for the twelve (3:14 has it in some manuscripts); the trapdoor says 'the only place'. Confirm or soften.
The Eucharistic reading of the feeding (CCC 1335) stated as what Catholics hear in it.
